newsitem.title: UK: Brazil global bond spread hit by Mexican peso woes.
newsitem.headline: Brazil global bond spread hit by Mexican peso woes.

text.p: Brazil's $750 million five-year global bond was put under pressure by the latest bout of weakness in the Mexican peso, dealers said on Thursday.

The Brazil yield spread was around 285/275 basis points over U.S. Treasuries from 275 b.p. yesterday and 265 b.p. when the deal was launched on Monday. "The fact the peso closed above eight (per dollar) sparked nervousness," said one trader involved in the Brazil deal. He quoted the issue at 285/275 b.p. The peso closed above eight to the dollar for the first time on Wednesday amid a lack of confidence by foreign investors.
Another trader close to the Brazil deal said the rally in U.S. Treasuries was partly behind the spread widening.
Since the Brazil deal was priced on Monday by joint lead managers J.P. Morgan and SBC Warburg, the 10-year Treasury note yield has tightened around 15 b.p. to 6.40 percent.
All other things being equal, Eurobonds, typically, do not follow big moves in the U.S. Treasury market on a one-for-one basis, partly on the assumption they may be quickly reversed.
However, if the U.S. Treasury move proved durable, Eurobond spreads generally tighten in again.

The Brazil bond, its debut dollar global offering, was given an 8.875 percent coupon. After it was priced, a syndicate manager at SBC Warburg said it was sold around 40 percent into Asia, 20 percent into Europe, 20 percent into Latin America and 20 percent to the U.S..
SBC Warburg said it was encouraged to see such strong demand from Asian investors many of whom were new to the LatAm sector. SBC Warburg quoted the deal at 285/280 b.p. this morning.
Brazil is rated B1 by Moody's Investors Service and B+ by Standard and Poor's Corp.

Moody's global ratings guide says "Bonds which are rated B generally lack characteristics of the desirable investment. Assurance of interest and principal payments or of miantenance of other terms of the contract over any long period of time may be small".

S&P's ratings handbook says: "An obligor rated B...has the capacity to meet its financial commitments. Adverse business, financial or economic conditions will likely impair...obligor's capacity or willingness to meet its financial commitments".
